notes.meaning: Jesus arrives in Bethany six days before the Passover, starting His final week before the cross. He returns to the hometown of Lazarus, whom He had raised from the dead, willingly placing Himself within reach of His enemies.

A special dinner is given in honor of Jesus, likely to celebrate Lazarus being restored to life. Martha faithfully serves the food, while Lazarus reclines at the table as living proof of Christ's power.
Mary takes a whole pound of very costly nard perfume, pours it over Jesus' feet, and wipes them with her hair. Her generous and humble act fills the entire house with a sweet fragrance.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Latin Catholic tradition historically identified Mary of Bethany, Mary Magdalene, and the repentant sinner in Luke 7 as the same woman.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars hold that only John names this woman as Mary of Bethany, and that later Western tradition mistakenly merged several distinct women into one.

notes.meaning: Judas Iscariot speaks up to object to Mary's loving deed. John notes that Judas was the disciple who would soon betray Jesus, contrasting his cold heart with Mary's sincere devotion.

Judas asks why the perfume was not sold for three hundred denarii, about a full year's wages for a laborer, and given to the poor. He hides his selfish complaint behind an excuse of caring for the needy.
Judas did not actually care about the poor at all. He held the money bag for Jesus and the disciples, and he was secretly stealing the money placed into it.
Jesus tells Judas to leave Mary alone and defends her loving action. He explains that she has kept and poured this costly oil in preparation for the day of His burial.

Jesus reminds His disciples that poor people will always be near them to receive help, but His bodily presence with them will soon end. Mary seized the moment to show Him honour while He was still alive.
A large crowd of Jewish pilgrims learns that Jesus is in Bethany and comes out to see Him. They also come to look at Lazarus, eager to see a man who had been raised from the dead.
The chief priests make plans to put Lazarus to death as well as Jesus. Because Lazarus was living proof of Christ's power, many people were leaving the religious leaders and trusting in Jesus.

The next day, the large crowd that had traveled to Jerusalem for the feast hears that Jesus is coming into the city. Many of these pilgrims had heard Him preach in the countryside and were eager to welcome Him.

The people take palm branches, symbols of victory and joy, and go out to meet Jesus as their king. They shout 'Hosanna,' a Hebrew word meaning 'Save now,' greeting Him from Psalm 118 as the Messiah who comes in the name of the Lord.

Jesus finds a young donkey and rides it into Jerusalem, directly fulfilling the prophecy written in Zechariah. Instead of riding a war horse like an earthly ruler, He comes gently as the Prince of Peace.

The disciples did not understand the meaning of these events while they were happening. Only after Jesus rose from the dead and ascended to glory did they remember that the Scriptures had foretold these very things.
The people who had witnessed Jesus call Lazarus out of the tomb kept telling others what they had seen. Their eyewitness reports spread rapidly and excited the whole city.
The crowd went out to meet Jesus because they had heard about this great miracle. Raising a dead man after four days convinced many that Jesus truly was the promised King.
Seeing the huge crowds, the frustrated Pharisees tell one another that their schemes have achieved nothing. In their anger, they exclaim that the whole world has gone after Jesus.
Some Greeks were among the travelers who had come up to worship the true God at the Passover feast. These Gentiles seeking God foreshadowed the nations coming to faith in Christ.
These Greeks approach Philip, who had a Greek name and came from Galilee, with a polite request. They ask for an interview because they want to meet and learn from Jesus.
Philip goes to consult with Andrew about whether to introduce these Gentiles to Jesus. The two disciples then go together and take the request to the Lord.
Jesus replies that the set time has finally come for the Son of Man to be glorified. He sees the arrival of these Gentiles as a sign that His death and triumph on the cross are now at hand.
Jesus compares His life to a single kernel of wheat planted in the ground. Unless a seed falls into the soil and dies, it stays alone; but when it dies, it springs up to produce a large harvest.
Jesus teaches that anyone who clings greedily to this earthly life will end up losing it. But whoever is willing to let go of this world to follow Christ will keep their life forever.
